extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters (court and legal reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Examples and case-based excerpts illustrating how to report criminal and civil court proceedings, judicial decisions, and related legal news for newspaper audiences. Includes factual narrative, legal holdings, procedural outcomes, and background context used in court reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer liability for servant's acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of liability depends upon whether the injury was committed by the authority of the master, expressly conferred, or fairly inferable from the nature of the employment; if a servant acts maliciously or outside the scope of his employment, the master is not responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from the Appellate Division opinion: 'If a servant goes outside of his employment and, without regard to his service, acting maliciously or in order to effect some purpose of his own, wantonly commits a trespass or causes damage to another, the master is not responsible.' Applied to facts where a driver assaulted another driver while not performing duties; the court reversed lower-court finding of employer liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal expatriation law (effect on married women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the federal expatriation law of 1907 (as construed by the Supreme Court in Mrs. Ethel Coope Mackenzie's case), a woman born in the United States who becomes the wife of a foreigner automatically relinquishes her U.S. citizenship and voting rights the moment she becomes the wife of a foreigner, whether the foreigner is a resident or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ruling applied broadly to women married to non-citizens; the article notes practical consequence (loss of voting right) and that the husband's naturalization could restore her citizenship. Presented as the legal holding and social implications (especially for suffrage activists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess fare refund requirement under two-cent fare law
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess fare cannot be legally collected from a passenger on Wisconsin railroads when tickets are purchased on trains unless provision is made to refund the amount of the overcharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General P. L. Gilbert's opinion reasons that the two-cent fare law established a maximum passenger rate and that any excess retained by a carrier is unlawful unless a refund mechanism exists or the legislature authorizes collection/retention as a penalty. Context: prior practice charged an additional amount (10 cents) when fares paid on train; railroads sought commission/clarification from the railroad commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity commitment and conservatorship procedure/effects (Illinois example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical officer may examine and recommend commitment; a jury (in this instance composed of one physician) may return a verdict of insanity; the court may appoint a conservator for the person's money and commit the person to a state hospital. The conservatorship and the official record of insanity may remain for a fixed statutory period (here noted as one year), during which the conservator cannot be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Baptiste Bardoli was examined by an assistant city physician who recommended commitment; a jury found 'alcoholic hallucinosis,' county judge appointed a conservator and committed him to the state hospital; later courts restored rights and funds, but records still show insanity for a year and conservator tenure lasts a year under Illinois law as cited in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for receivership and receiver powers in corporate insolvency
rubrics_metrics.description: Receivership may be sought by creditors (here, banks) upon discovery of misleading or inflated reports (e.g., inflated branch sales leading to misleading annual statements). A receiver is appointed to protect creditors, may seek fullest authority to conduct the business (especially where perishable goods are involved), can appoint ancillary receivers for branch plants, and can employ auditors to investigate finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case facts: Robert Z. Link & Co. faced receivership after banks discovered misleading sales statements; receiver pursued powers to preserve perishable inventory, convened with railroads about goods in transit, and engaged auditors. The narrative emphasizes causes (lack of internal checks on managers' reported sales) and practical receiver actions (securing authority, investigating use of preferred stock proceeds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal liability for sidewalk defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipality may be held liable for injuries caused by defective sidewalk conditions (in this account, an elevated sidewalk unprotected by a rail) where the city's negligence in maintaining safe sidewalks is shown and a jury award is affirmed by the higher court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Florence Lemoine's $5,000 verdict against the city for a fall from an elevated, unprotected sidewalk was upheld by the Minnesota supreme court; the article gives facts (location, condition of sidewalk, injuries) and emphasizes the court's affirmation of municipal liability in such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory punishment for grand larceny in second degree (case example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grand larceny in the second degree (here, under an indictment charging defrauding a railroad company of $1,000) is punishable by imprisonment in the state penitentiary from one to ten years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: jury found defendant guilty in nine minutes; narrative includes description of the defendant's scheme (faking paralysis), prior aliases and convictions, and a note that sentence will be imposed later. The statutory range is cited as part of the reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate internal controls and checking of branch reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should implement systems to check and verify reported sales from branch managers; failure to do so can lead to misleading annual statements and financial crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Link & Co. example, ambitious branch managers allegedly inflated sales to increase commission; the company had no system of checking these reports, and the discrepancies were discovered only after bankers put an auditing firm on the books. Presented as a causal factor in the receivership and a governance lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment for benefit of creditors as a remedy for insolvent firms
rubrics_metrics.description: An insolvent business may assign its assets for the benefit of creditors to a designated assignee/receiver (example: H. W. Williams assigned for the benefit of creditors to Mark T. Cox), with liabilities estimated and creditors represented by attorneys; assignment is a step to protect creditor interests and facilitate settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example notes no immediate complications expected for other Wall Street houses and gives estimated liability ranges. Reporting includes who the assignee is and mentions counsel for principal creditors, illustrating typical reporting elements for such an assignment.
